ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Antibiotic principles and resistance: 4

A patient has recurrent infection around an implanted device despite an antibiotic active against the organism in standard culture. The bacteria are embedded in an adherent matrix. Which persistence mechanism helps explain the need to assess device removal?

  1. Reduced outer-membrane permeability
  2. Biofilm-associated persistence
  3. Enzymatic drug inactivation
  4. Modification of the drug target
  5. Increased drug efflux
Answer and explanation

Biofilm-associated persistence

Organisms in biofilms can be difficult to eradicate; device management may be needed despite planktonic susceptibility.

Option explanations

Biofilm-associated persistence: Organisms in biofilms can be difficult to eradicate; device management may be needed despite planktonic susceptibility.

Enzymatic drug inactivation: Bacteria can produce enzymes that destroy or chemically modify an antibiotic. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Modification of the drug target: A changed target can bind the antibiotic less effectively while maintaining its microbial function. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Increased drug efflux: Transport pumps can lower intracellular antibiotic exposure. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Reduced outer-membrane permeability: Loss or alteration of porins can reduce entry of antibiotics into Gram-negative bacteria. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
